hypotheses.title: Anyone can grant/revoke CONTROLLER role via unprotected addController/removeController
hypotheses.description: `addController(address)` and `removeController(address)` call `grantRole(CONTROLLER, ...)` / `revokeRole(CONTROLLER, ...)` but have no access modifier. Any external caller can grant themselves the CONTROLLER role, which lets them invoke `safetySwitch()` to halt minting/burning (and any other CONTROLLER-gated logic), or revoke legitimate controllers.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls `addController(attacker)` — succeeds because no `onlyRole` check. 2) Attacker now holds CONTROLLER. 3) Attacker calls `safetySwitch()` to flip `_operating` to false, disabling mint/burn for the whole system. 4) Attacker can also call `removeController(legitController)` to strip legitimate controllers.
hypotheses.impact: Complete denial of service on minting/burning; attacker can permanently lock the operating state (only DEFAULT_ADMIN or the recorded `_operatingController` can re-enable, and attacker can re-flip repeatedly). Loss of availability of core token operations.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add `onlyRole(DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE)` (or appropriate admin role) to `addController` and `removeController`.

hypotheses.title: Anyone can add/remove minters and set arbitrary mint allowances
hypotheses.description: `addMinter(address,uint256)` and `removeMinter(address)` have no access modifier. Any external caller can grant `MINTER_ROLE` to an arbitrary address with an arbitrary `minterAllowed` amount, enabling unlimited minting (up to the allowance) of the token.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls `addMinter(attacker, type(uint256).max)`. 2) Attacker now has MINTER_ROLE with max allowance. 3) Attacker calls `mint(attacker, hugeAmount)` (assuming `_operating` is true) to mint tokens to themselves. 4) Attacker dumps tokens for value.
hypotheses.impact: Unlimited inflation of token supply, draining of any liquidity/pools, complete loss of token value and protocol solvency.
hypotheses.recommendation: Restrict `addMinter`/`removeMinter` to `onlyRole(MASTER_MINTER)` (or DEFAULT_ADMIN).

hypotheses.title: Anyone can replace the MASTER_MINTER role
hypotheses.description: `setMasterMinter(address)` has no access modifier. Any external caller can revoke the current MASTER_MINTER and grant the role to an arbitrary address (including themselves), taking over the minter-management hierarchy.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls `setMasterMinter(attacker)`. 2) The current master minter is revoked and attacker is granted MASTER_MINTER. 3) Attacker now controls `updateMintingAllowance`, `addMinter`, `removeMinter`, and can mint directly (MASTER_MINTER bypasses allowance in `mint`).
hypotheses.impact: Full takeover of minting authority; unlimited token minting; total loss of token integrity.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add `onlyRole(DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE)` to `setMasterMinter`.

hypotheses.title: ERC20ControlerMinterUpgradeable.mint allows MASTER_MINTER unlimited minting bypassing allowance
hypotheses.description: The `mint` function checks `if (!hasRole(MASTER_MINTER, _msgSender()) && !hasRole(MINTER_ROLE, _msgSender())) revert NotMinter`. If the caller has `MASTER_MINTER`, the allowance check `if (hasRole(MINTER_ROLE, _msgSender()))` is skipped entirely, so a MASTER_MINTER can mint an unbounded amount. While MASTER_MINTER is a trusted role, the `setMasterMinter` function grants MASTER_MINTER to a new address and revokes the old one, but `_grantRole(MASTER_MINTER, address(0))` in `__ERC20ControlerMinter_init_unchained` grants the role to address(0), which is a known anti-pattern. More critically, `addController`/`removeController` are callable by anyone (no access modifier), allowing any external actor to grant themselves CONTROLLER role and then call `safetySwitch` to toggle operating state.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls `addController(attacker)` — no access control. 2) Attacker now has CONTROLLER role. 3) Attacker calls `safetySwitch()` to set `_operating = false`, halting all minting and burning. 4) Attacker can also call `safetySwitch()` again only if they are DEFAULT_ADMIN or the operating controller; but the initial toggle is free.
hypotheses.impact: Any external actor can grant themselves CONTROLLER and halt minting/burning (DoS), or manipulate operating state. If combined with other role grants, could lead to unauthorized minting.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add `onlyRole(DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE)` or `onlyRole(MASTER_MINTER)` to `addController` and `removeController`.

hypotheses.title: Anyone can set the trusted forwarder on the token
hypotheses.description: `setTrustedForwarder(address)` in `ERC20MetaTxUpgradeable` is `public virtual` with no access control. `EURFToken` overrides it with `onlyRole(ADMIN)`, but the base contract is inherited by other contracts and the override only protects the derived path. More critically, `_msgSender()` trusts the last 20 bytes of calldata whenever `msg.sender == _trustedForwarder`, so an attacker who can set the forwarder can spoof any `_msgSender()`.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls `setTrustedForwarder(attacker)` on any contract that inherits the base without overriding (or via any path that reaches the base). 2) Attacker then calls token functions from `attacker` address; `_msgSender()` returns the appended 20 bytes, letting attacker impersonate any address (e.g., a whale or the owner) for `transfer`, `permit`, `transferWithAuthorization`, `mint`, `burn`, `forceTransfer`, etc.
hypotheses.impact: Full impersonation of arbitrary accounts; theft of balances via `transfer`/`transferFrom`/`transferWithAuthorization`; unauthorized mint/burn/admin actions.
hypotheses.recommendation: Make `setTrustedForwarder` `internal` or gate it with `onlyRole(ADMIN)` in the base contract itself.

hypotheses.title: Forwarder.initialize can be front-run to hijack ownership and token binding
hypotheses.description: `initialize(address)` is `public initializer` with no restriction on who may call it first. An attacker can front-run the legitimate deployment/initialization transaction and become the owner, and set `_eurfAddress`/`_eurf` to an attacker-controlled token contract.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes the pending `initialize` tx (or simply calls it first after deployment). 2) Attacker calls `initialize(attackerToken)`. 3) Attacker becomes owner (via `__Ownable_init(_msgSender())`) and sets `_eurf` to their malicious contract. 4) Attacker can then call `registerRequestType` (owner-only) and, more importantly, `execute` will forward `transfer` calls to the attacker's token, and `payGaslessBasefee` will be invoked on the attacker's contract.
hypotheses.impact: Ownership hijack of the Forwarder; the forwarder is bound to a malicious token, enabling arbitrary behavior on `execute` (including draining value sent with `req.value` to attacker-controlled code).
hypotheses.recommendation: Use `initializer` combined with an `onlyOwner`-style deployer check, or initialize atomically in the constructor/proxy deploy script; consider `reinitializer` guards and setting `_eurfAddress` immutably.

hypotheses.title: calculateTxFee rounds down, allowing zero-fee dust transfers
hypotheses.description: `calculateTxFee` computes `(txAmount * _txfeeRate) / FEE_RATIO`. For small `txAmount` such that `txAmount * _txfeeRate < FEE_RATIO`, the fee is zero. An attacker can split a large transfer into many small transfers, each below the threshold, to avoid paying any fees. For example, with `_txfeeRate = 1` (0.01%), any transfer of less than 10000 units (0.01 EURF with 6 decimals) pays zero fee. This is a rounding-down issue that favors the user over the protocol.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker wants to transfer 1000 EURF. 2. Instead of one transfer, attacker makes 100,000 transfers of 0.01 EURF each. 3. Each transfer has `txAmount * 1 / 10000 = 0`, so no fee is paid. 4. Attacker avoids all fees. Gas costs may make this impractical on mainnet, but on L2 or with subsidized gas, it's viable.
hypotheses.impact: Protocol loses fee revenue; fee mechanism can be bypassed entirely for small amounts.
hypotheses.recommendation: Enforce a minimum fee (e.g., `max(1, calculatedFee)`) or require `txAmount` to be above a threshold for fee-free transfers.

hypotheses.title: Forwarder signature not bound to contract address or chain id, enabling cross-deployment replay
hypotheses.description: The Forwarder trusts the `domainSeparator` provided as a call argument and does not verify it against an internally computed value derived from `address(this)` and `block.chainid`. The signed struct in `_getEncoded` also omits the Ethereum chain id, the Forwarder's own address, and the target token address. As a result, a signature produced for one Forwarder deployment is valid on any other Forwarder deployment (same chain or another chain) with the same `_eurfAddress`, since nonces are stored per-Forwarder and are initially zero.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Signer signs a ForwardRequest for Forwarder A. 2) Attacker deploys (or reuses) Forwarder B on the same or a different chain, initialized with a token whose address equals `req.to`. 3) Attacker submits the signed request to B with the same `domainSeparator` (which the signer's off-chain domain used, or which matches by construction). 4) `_verifyNonce` passes (fresh nonce), `_verifySig` recovers `req.from`, `_updateNonce` advances. 5) Token transfer executes on B's `_eurfAddress`, debiting signer, crediting the attacker-chosen recipient embedded in `req.data`—but for B's token, the signer's balance there may differ; if same token address via CREATE2, balance is shared. Realistically, cross-chain replay to a Forwarder controlling the same token is the concrete exploit.
hypotheses.impact: Unauthorized token transfers from signer by replaying a single signature on another Forwarder deployment/chain; drains signer's token balance.
hypotheses.recommendation: Compute the EIP-712 domain separator internally from `block.chainid` and `address(this)` (or verify the passed value equals the internally computed one), and include chain id and verifying contract in the signed payload.

hypotheses.title: ERC20MetaTxUpgradeable.transferWithAuthorization uses non-standard TWA typehash and no chain binding
hypotheses.description: The `_TWA_TYPEHASH` is defined as `TransferWithAuthorization(address owner,address spender,uint256 value,uint256 nonce,uint256 deadline)`, which does not match the EIP-3009 standard (which uses `from`, `to`, `value`, `validAfter`, `validBefore`, `nonce`). More importantly, the function transfers from `holder` to `spender` (treating `spender` as recipient), which is a non-standard semantic. The signature is bound to the EIP-712 domain via `_hashTypedDataV4`, but the domain is set once at initialization with `name` and `"1"` and never includes `block.chainid` explicitly beyond OZ's default (which does include chainid). However, the nonce is consumed via `_useNonce(holder)` before signature verification, so a failed signature still burns the nonce — a griefing vector.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker front-runs a legitimate `transferWithAuthorization` call by submitting it with a bad signature (or any call that reaches `_useNonce`). 2) `_useNonce(holder)` increments the nonce before `ECDSA.recover` is checked. 3) The legitimate signed transaction now has a stale nonce and reverts, permanently invalidating the user's signed authorization.
hypotheses.impact: Denial of service on meta-transactions; user's signed authorizations become unusable, and the user must re-sign with a new nonce.
hypotheses.recommendation: Move `_useNonce` after signature verification, or use a try/revert pattern that only consumes the nonce on success.

hypotheses.title: Forwarder signed request has no deadline, so signed meta-transactions live forever
hypotheses.description: `ForwardRequest` contains no `deadline` (and no block/timestamp), and `_getEncoded` does not include any time bound. Nonces only prevent double-execution, not delayed execution. A signed request that a signer intended for the current token configuration (fee rate, blacklist state, `_gaslessBasefee`, trusted forwarder) remains executable indefinitely until the nonce is consumed, which lets an attacker wait for a state change that benefits them.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker obtains a signed ForwardRequest but does not submit it. 2) Admin later raises `_gaslessBasefee` or `_txfeeRate`, or changes blacklist/pause state. 3) Attacker submits the now-stale signed request; it still validates because no deadline is signed. 4) Signer pays the updated fee, or the transfer executes under conditions the signer never agreed to.
hypotheses.impact: Signer can be forced to execute a stale transfer under materially different fee/state conditions, causing unexpected fee loss or execution that the signer would have revoked.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add a `deadline` (and optionally block-number bound) to `ForwardRequest`, include it in `_getEncoded`, and revert in `execute` when `block.timestamp > deadline`.

hypotheses.title: payGaslessBasefee can be replayed to drain payer via repeated forwarder calls
hypotheses.description: `execute` verifies the nonce and signature, then calls `_eurf.payGaslessBasefee(req.from, _msgSender())` which transfers `_gaslessBasefee` from `req.from` to the caller. The nonce is incremented per `req.from`, but the same signed request cannot be replayed; however, any party can call `execute` with a valid signed request and become the paymaster, collecting the basefee. Since the signature only authorizes the transfer data (not the paymaster), a front-runner can intercept a pending signed request and claim the gasless basefee for themselves.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Victim signs a `ForwardRequest` for a transfer and broadcasts it. 2) Attacker observes the pending tx in the mempool. 3) Attacker front-runs by calling `execute` with the same signed request, becoming `_msgSender()` (paymaster). 4) Attacker receives `_gaslessBasefee` from the victim instead of the intended relayer.
hypotheses.impact: The intended relayer/paymaster loses the gasless basefee reward; attacker steals the fee from the victim's balance.
hypotheses.recommendation: Include the paymaster address in the signed request struct so the signature binds the intended recipient of the basefee.

hypotheses.title: Forwarder.execute forwards arbitrary calldata via abi.encodePacked allowing selector bypass
hypotheses.description: The check `bytes4(req.data[:4]) == transferSelector` only inspects the first 4 bytes of `req.data`, but the actual call is made with `abi.encodePacked(req.data, req.from)`. Because `req.data` is attacker-controlled and appended with `req.from`, the calldata passed to the token can be crafted so that the first 4 bytes match `transfer(address,uint256)` while the trailing bytes shift the argument decoding. Specifically, `abi.encodePacked` concatenates without length padding, so a `req.data` of exactly 4 bytes (just the selector) followed by 20 bytes of `req.from` produces a valid `transfer(address,uint256)` call where the recipient is `req.from` and the amount is read from the next 32 bytes — which are absent, causing the call to revert or, with crafted padding, to misroute funds. More critically, the signature is verified over `keccak256(req.data)` but the executed calldata is `req.data || req.from`, so the signed payload and executed payload differ.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker crafts `req.data` = `transfer(address,uint256)` selector + 32 bytes of attacker-chosen amount, with `req.from` = victim. 2) The signature is over `req.data` only, so the attacker signs (or tricks victim into signing) a payload whose executed form appends `req.from` as extra calldata. 3) Because `abi.encodePacked` appends `req.from` after the 36-byte transfer calldata, the EVM ignores trailing bytes for `transfer`, so the call succeeds but the signed digest does not bind the actual recipient/amount semantics as intended. 4) Attacker can also exploit the mismatch between signed `req.data` and executed `req.data || req.from` to replay or redirect.
hypotheses.impact: Signature does not bind the full executed calldata; attacker can cause transfers inconsistent with what the signer authorized, leading to unauthorized token movement from the signer's balance.
hypotheses.recommendation: Verify the signature over the exact calldata that will be executed (including `req.from`), or use `abi.encodeWithSelector` and validate the decoded recipient/amount against `req.from` and signed fields.

hypotheses.title: payGaslessBasefee can be replayed to drain payer via forwarder
hypotheses.description: `payGaslessBasefee` is called by the Forwarder after executing a meta-transaction. It transfers `_gaslessBasefee` from `payer` to `paymaster` (the caller of the forwarder). The Forwarder's `execute` verifies the nonce and signature, but `payGaslessBasefee` itself only checks `isTrustedForwarder(msg.sender)`. If the trusted forwarder is set, any call path through the forwarder that reaches `payGaslessBasefee` will charge the payer. Since the forwarder only allows `transfer(address,uint256)` selector, the `payGaslessBasefee` call is made directly by the forwarder after the transfer. However, the forwarder's `execute` does not verify that the `req.from` matches the actual signer of the transfer data — it does verify the signature over the request, but the `req.data` is `transfer(recipient, amount)` and the `req.from` is appended. The payer is `req.from`. An attacker who obtains a valid signed request (e.g., from mempool) can front-run and execute it, becoming the `paymaster` and collecting the gasless basefee. This is intended (paymaster is the executor), but the payer pays the basefee regardless of whether the transfer succeeds or the recipient is correct. More critically, if `_gaslessBasefee` is set and the payer has balance, any executor can claim it. This is by design but can be abused if the signed request is replayed across chains or if the nonce is not properly domain-separated.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker observes a signed meta-transaction in the mempool. 2. Attacker calls `Forwarder.execute` with the same request and signature. 3. Forwarder verifies nonce and signature, executes the transfer, then calls `payGaslessBasefee(req.from, attacker)`. 4. Attacker receives `_gaslessBasefee` from the payer. The original intended executor loses the reward. This is a front-running/griefing attack.
hypotheses.impact: The intended paymaster loses the gasless basefee reward; the payer pays the same amount but to the attacker. No direct loss to the payer beyond what was signed, but the reward is stolen from the legitimate executor.
hypotheses.recommendation: Include the paymaster address in the signed request or use a commit-reveal scheme to prevent front-running of meta-transactions.

hypotheses.title: Forwarder._verifySig lacks EIP-712 domain separator binding to contract address and chainid
hypotheses.description: The `domainSeparator` is an external input. Even if the signer uses EIP-712 with a proper domain (chainId, address), the contract does not enforce that the supplied `domainSeparator` matches an internally computed one. Because the same signer may sign for multiple Forwarders (or the same code deployed at different addresses), a valid signature for one Forwarder is valid for another when the caller supplies the same `domainSeparator`. Combined with per-contract nonces, this enables signature replay across Forwarder deployments.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker obtains a signed ForwardRequest whose `domainSeparator` corresponds to Forwarder contract F1 including `address(F1)` and `chainid`. 2) Attacker deploys Forwarder F2 on the same chain (or same contract on another chain where `chainid` doesn't change for the signer's domain—if signer used a fixed domain). 3) If signer signed with a domain that is not F2-specific, F2 accepts the same sig since it only checks `digest.recover(sig) == req.from`. 4) Token transfer executes on F2's `_eurfAddress`.
hypotheses.impact: Unauthorized token transfers signing once but executing on multiple deployments.
hypotheses.recommendation: Compute the domain separator on-chain via `_domainSeparatorV4` or verify the passed value equals an internal `keccak256` over the EIP-712 domain derived from `address(this)` and `block.chainid`.

hypotheses.title: Fee-on-transfer double-charges sender via transferWithAuthorization path
hypotheses.description: `transferWithAuthorization` calls `transferSanity(holder, spender, value)` which invokes `_payTxFee(holder, value)` charging the fee, then calls `super.transferWithAuthorization` which performs `_update(holder, spender, value)`. The fee is deducted from `holder` but the full `value` is still transferred, so the sender pays `value + fee` while the recipient receives `value`. This is inconsistent with `transfer`/`transferFrom` where the fee is also charged on top, but here the meta-tx path is signed by the holder for exactly `value`, so the holder's balance is silently drained beyond the signed amount.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker obtains a signed `transferWithAuthorization` from a victim (e.g., via a relayer/marketplace that expects only `value` to leave the victim). 2) Attacker submits it when `_txfeeRate > 0`. 3) Victim is charged `value + fee` even though the signature authorized only `value`. 4) Attacker repeats with any other signed authorizations to drain extra fees from victims.
hypotheses.impact: Victims lose more tokens than they signed for; fee accounting diverges from the signed intent; potential loss of funds.
hypotheses.recommendation: Charge the fee from the transferred amount (deduct from `value`) or require the signature to cover `value + fee` explicitly.

hypotheses.title: Gasless basefee paid even when transfer amount is zero or fails silently
hypotheses.description: `execute` calls `_eurf.payGaslessBasefee(req.from, _msgSender())` after the low-level call succeeds. The low-level call uses `abi.encodePacked(req.data, req.from)` which appends the `from` address to the calldata. For `transfer(address,uint256)`, this means the recipient is `req.from` (the signer), so the signer transfers to themselves — a no-op transfer — yet still pays the gasless basefee to the paymaster. An attacker can craft a signed request where `req.data` encodes a transfer to the signer themselves, and the paymaster collects the basefee for a meaningless transfer.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker obtains any valid signed `ForwardRequest` from a victim (e.g., via phishing or a marketplace). 2) Attacker calls `execute`; the transfer is a self-transfer (no value moves) but `payGaslessBasefee` still charges the victim. 3) Attacker collects the basefee repeatedly if multiple signed requests exist.
hypotheses.impact: Victim's balance drained by basefee for no-op transfers; attacker profits.
hypotheses.recommendation: Validate that the transfer recipient differs from `req.from`, or require the signed request to specify the actual recipient explicitly.

hypotheses.title: Fee-on-transfer double-charges sender, breaking balance accounting
hypotheses.description: `transferSanity` calls `_payTxFee(sender, amount)` which transfers `txFees` from `sender` to `_feesFaucet` BEFORE `super.transfer(recipient, amount)` moves the full `amount` from `sender` to `recipient`. The sanity check `balanceOf(from) < txFees + txAmount` is performed, but the fee is deducted from the sender's balance and then the full `amount` is also deducted, so the sender effectively pays `amount + txFees`. This is intended, but the check uses `txFees + txAmount` while the actual deduction is exactly that — however, the fee is computed on `txAmount` and the recipient receives the full `txAmount`, meaning the fee is an extra charge on top of the transfer, not deducted from it. If the sender's balance is exactly `txFees + txAmount`, the transfer succeeds and drains the sender completely, which is fine, but the fee is silently taken from the sender's remaining balance rather than from the transferred amount, which can cause unexpected balance drift for integrators expecting fee-on-transfer semantics.
hypotheses.attackPath: Not directly exploitable by an untrusted actor; this is a design/accounting mismatch. However, a recipient or sender relying on standard fee-on-transfer semantics (recipient receives `amount - fee`) will be surprised: the recipient receives the full `amount` and the sender is debited `amount + fee`. An attacker cannot directly exploit this, but it can be used to grief: a sender with balance exactly `amount` (no room for fee) will have their transfer revert, while a sender with `amount + fee` will lose the fee unexpectedly.
hypotheses.impact: Sender loses more than expected; integrators mis-account balances; potential for failed transfers when balance is between `amount` and `amount + fee`.
hypotheses.recommendation: Deduct the fee from the transferred amount (recipient receives `amount - fee`) or clearly document that the fee is additive and adjust the sanity check accordingly.

hypotheses.title: Forwarder.execute lacks replay protection across chains/domains and nonce is per-from only
hypotheses.description: `_verifySig` uses a caller-supplied `domainSeparator` and `requestTypeHash` without validating them against the contract's own EIP-712 domain or a whitelist beyond `typeHashes[requestTypeHash]`. Any registered typehash is accepted, and the domain separator is fully attacker-controlled. Combined with the nonce being tracked only per `req.from` inside this Forwarder, a signature valid on one deployment/chain can be replayed on another deployment of the same Forwarder where the same `req.from` nonce is still unused.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes a signed `ForwardRequest` on chain A (or a fork/testnet) with `req.from = victim`. 2) Attacker submits the same request on chain B's Forwarder deployment where `nonces[victim]` is still 0. 3) `_verifyNonce` passes, `_verifySig` passes because the attacker supplies the same `domainSeparator` and a registered `requestTypeHash`, and the transfer executes again.
hypotheses.impact: Replay of signed meta-transactions across chains/deployments, causing duplicate token transfers and gasless basefee charges from the victim.
hypotheses.recommendation: Bind the domain separator to `address(this)` and `block.chainid` (use OZ EIP712), and reject any `domainSeparator` not equal to the locally computed one.

hypotheses.title: EURFToken.payGaslessBasefee charges fixed basefee regardless of actual gas, enabling griefing
hypotheses.description: `payGaslessBasefee` transfers a fixed `_gaslessBasefee` amount from `payer` to `paymaster` whenever called by the trusted forwarder. The amount is set by ADMIN and is not tied to actual gas consumed, gas price, or any oracle. A malicious paymaster (any external actor who is a trusted forwarder's relayer) can repeatedly call `Forwarder.execute` with minimal-gas transfers, draining the payer's balance at the fixed basefee rate far exceeding real gas costs. There is no per-epoch cap, no refund of excess, and no check that the payer authorized this specific paymaster.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker registers as a relayer/paymaster (any address can be `_msgSender()` in `execute`). 2) Attacker obtains a valid signed `ForwardRequest` from victim (e.g., a small transfer). 3) Attacker calls `execute`, which calls `payGaslessBasefee(victim, attacker)`, transferring `_gaslessBasefee` to attacker. 4) Attacker repeats with many small transfers, extracting the fixed fee each time regardless of actual gas used.
hypotheses.impact: Victim's token balance drained via repeated fixed-fee charges disproportionate to actual gas; wrong accounting of gasless fees.
hypotheses.recommendation: Compute the basefee from actual gas used and a gas-price oracle, or cap total fees per epoch and require explicit payer authorization of the paymaster.

hypotheses.title: EURFToken.transferWithAuthorization lacks nonce binding to spender allowing replay
hypotheses.description: `transferWithAuthorization` computes the struct hash using `_useNonce(holder)` which increments the holder's nonce, but the nonce is consumed inside the hash computation before signature verification. If the signature is invalid, the nonce is still incremented (state change before check), allowing an attacker to grief a holder by submitting invalid signatures that consume nonces, or to front-run a legitimate authorization by consuming the nonce first. Additionally, `_update` is called after signature verification but the nonce increment happens before, so a reentrant call via a token hook (if the token were ERC777-like) could observe the incremented nonce.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes a pending `transferWithAuthorization` in the mempool. 2) Attacker submits the same signed authorization first (front-running) — since nonce is consumed on first valid call, the victim's tx reverts. 3) Alternatively, attacker submits invalid signatures repeatedly to burn the victim's nonces, causing all future authorizations to fail.
hypotheses.impact: Denial of service on the victim's meta-transactions; nonce desynchronization; frozen funds if the victim relies on off-chain signed authorizations.
hypotheses.recommendation: Verify the signature first, then consume the nonce; or use a nonce mapping that is only incremented on successful verification.

hypotheses.title: Blacklisted recipient permanently blocks all transfers to that address
hypotheses.description: `adminSanity` reverts with `RecipientBlacklistedError` whenever `to` is blacklisted, and this check runs on every transfer path (transfer, transferFrom, transferWithAuthorization, forceTransfer). An admin blacklisting an address that is a common recipient (e.g., a DEX pool, bridge, or fee faucet) causes every transfer targeting that address to revert, freezing the ability of all users to interact with that destination. There is no user-side recovery path; only the admin can unblacklist.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Admin blacklists a widely-used recipient (or an attacker who is also an admin colludes). 2) All users attempting to transfer to that address revert. 3) Funds already held by that address cannot be moved out via normal transfer because `from` is also checked when the sender is not admin. 4) Users are stuck until admin acts.
hypotheses.impact: Frozen funds and blocked transfers for any user whose counterparty is blacklisted; potential permanent lock if admin key is lost.
hypotheses.recommendation: Allow the blacklisted account itself to transfer out (only block incoming), or provide a user-triggered escape path.

hypotheses.title: Forwarder.execute appends req.from to calldata, corrupting transfer args
hypotheses.description: The forwarder builds the inner call as `abi.encodePacked(req.data, req.from)`, appending the 20-byte `from` address to the already-encoded `transfer(address,uint256)` calldata. The token's `transfer` reads only the first 4+32+32 bytes, so the trailing 20 bytes are ignored by the EVM ABI decoder, but the intent (passing `from` as an argument) is wrong and the appended bytes are dead weight. More importantly, the token's `_msgSender()` override reads the last 20 bytes of calldata when `msg.sender` is the trusted forwarder — so the appended `req.from` is what makes the token see the signer as the sender. This coupling is fragile: any change to the token's `_msgSender` (or a non-conforming token) silently breaks the forwarder, and the `verify()` function does not enforce that `req.from` matches the actual signer's intent beyond the signature check.
hypotheses.attackPath: An attacker who obtains a valid signature for a `transfer` request can craft `req.data` such that the appended `req.from` is the signer, but the `to`/`amount` in `req.data` differ from what the signer believed — the signature covers `keccak256(req.data)` so this is bound, but the forwarder does not validate that `req.data` decodes to a `transfer` with the signer as the effective sender beyond the selector check. If the token's `_msgSender` logic is ever bypassed (e.g., direct call to token), the appended bytes are meaningless.
hypotheses.impact: Broken meta-transaction semantics; potential for the token to attribute the transfer to the wrong sender if the forwarder/token integration drifts, leading to unauthorized transfers from the signer's balance.
hypotheses.recommendation: Encode the inner call explicitly as `abi.encodeWithSelector(transferSelector, req.to, amount)` and pass `req.from` via a dedicated mechanism (e.g., the token's trusted-forwarder calldata suffix) rather than `abi.encodePacked` on raw calldata.

hypotheses.title: Fee charged on transferFrom even when allowance insufficient causes revert after fee
hypotheses.description: `transferFrom` calls `transferSanity(sender, recipient, amount)` which charges `_payTxFee(sender, amount)` before `super.transferFrom` checks the allowance. If the allowance is insufficient, the whole tx reverts, but if the allowance is exactly `amount` and the sender has enough balance for `amount + fee`, the fee is deducted and then the transfer succeeds. However, if the sender's balance is exactly `amount` (no room for fee), the fee payment reverts with `BalanceTooLow`, blocking legitimate transfers. More critically, the fee is charged on the sender even when the spender is the one initiating, which may not be the intended payer.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker (spender) calls `transferFrom(victim, attacker, amount)` where victim has exactly `amount` balance. 2) `_payTxFee` reverts due to insufficient balance for fee. 3) Victim's funds are effectively frozen for that amount until they acquire extra tokens for the fee. Alternatively, attacker can force fee deduction from victim on every transferFrom.
hypotheses.impact: Sender's balance is drained by fees on every spender-initiated transfer; users with exact balances cannot transfer.
hypotheses.recommendation: Deduct the fee from the transferred amount or from the spender, and document the payer clearly.

hypotheses.title: ERC20AdminUpgradeable.setAdministrator revokes ADMIN from index 0 without checking caller
hypotheses.description: `setAdministrator` is guarded by `onlyRole(DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE)`, but it revokes ADMIN from `getRoleMember(ADMIN, 0)` and grants to `newAdmin`. If `newAdmin` is already the sole ADMIN, `revokeRole` then `grantRole` is fine, but if `newAdmin` is address(0) or a contract that cannot use the role, ADMIN becomes unusable. More importantly, `__ERC20Admin_init_unchained` grants ADMIN to `address(0)`, so the initial ADMIN is address(0). Any DEFAULT_ADMIN can call `setAdministrator` to move ADMIN, but there is no check that `newAdmin != address(0)`, allowing ADMIN to be permanently locked to address(0).
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) A DEFAULT_ADMIN (trusted) calls `setAdministrator(address(0))`. 2) ADMIN role is now held only by address(0), which cannot call `pause`, `blacklist`, etc. 3) Protocol admin functions become unusable.
hypotheses.impact: Permanent loss of ADMIN functionality (pause, blacklist, fee configuration), freezing critical admin operations.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require `newAdmin != address(0)` and ensure `newAdmin` is not already the current ADMIN before revoking.

hypotheses.title: Forwarder.execute allows arbitrary calldata appended with attacker-controlled `from`
hypotheses.description: `execute` builds the calldata as `abi.encodePacked(req.data, req.from)` and forwards it to `req.to` (the EURF token). The signature only binds `keccak256(req.data)` and `req.from`, but the actual call appends `req.from` as a raw 20-byte suffix. Because `req.data` is only 4 bytes (selector) plus ABI-encoded args, the appended `from` becomes the third argument to `transfer(address,uint256)` — i.e., it is ignored by the token's `transfer` selector, but the token's `_msgSender()` override reads the last 20 bytes of calldata when the caller is the trusted forwarder. Thus the token sees `from` as the sender, not the actual signer. Combined with `_updateNonce` being called before the external call, a signed request can be replayed against a different `from` if the signature check is bypassed via the trusted-forwarder path.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker obtains any valid signed ForwardRequest (e.g., from mempool or a leaked signature) where `req.from = victim`. 2) Attacker calls `Forwarder.execute` with the same `req` but the token's `_msgSender()` resolves to `req.from` because the forwarder is trusted. 3) The token executes `transfer(recipient, amount)` debiting `req.from` (victim). 4) Nonce is incremented for `req.from`, but the attacker controls the recipient.
hypotheses.impact: Unauthorized transfer of victim's EURF tokens to attacker-controlled recipient; loss of funds.
hypotheses.recommendation: Do not append `req.from` to calldata; instead pass it explicitly as an ABI-encoded argument and validate the selector/args strictly, or use a dedicated meta-tx entrypoint on the token.

hypotheses.title: Pause blocks all non-admin transfers including withdrawals
hypotheses.description: When `paused()` is true, `adminSanity` reverts for any caller without ADMIN role, blocking transfer, transferFrom, and transferWithAuthorization. Users cannot move or withdraw their own tokens while paused; only admins can move funds via `forceTransfer`. If the admin key is lost or the pause is never lifted, all user funds are permanently frozen.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Admin (or compromised admin key) calls `pause()`. 2) Every non-admin transfer reverts with `PausedError`. 3) Users cannot withdraw, sell, or migrate their tokens. 4) No user-side unpause exists.
hypotheses.impact: Complete freeze of user funds during pause; permanent loss if admin is unavailable.
hypotheses.recommendation: Allow users to transfer/withdraw their own balances while paused, or add a timelock/escape hatch.

hypotheses.title: Forwarder execute reverts on zero-value transfer blocking meta-tx
hypotheses.description: `execute` calls `_eurf.payGaslessBasefee(req.from, _msgSender())` after the forwarded call. If `_gaslessBasefee` is greater than the payer's balance, `payGaslessBasefee` reverts with `BalanceTooLow`, causing the entire `execute` to revert even though the underlying transfer succeeded. A user with a balance smaller than the basefee cannot use the forwarder at all, and any meta-tx they sign will revert.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Admin sets `_gaslessBasefee` to a nonzero value. 2) A user with balance below that value signs a ForwardRequest. 3) Relayer calls `execute`; the inner transfer succeeds but `payGaslessBasefee` reverts. 4) The whole tx reverts, nonce is not consumed, and the user cannot use the forwarder.
hypotheses.impact: Meta-transaction path unusable for low-balance users; griefing vector if basefee is set high.
hypotheses.recommendation: Skip or cap the basefee payment when the payer's balance is insufficient, or check balance before reverting.

hypotheses.title: Forwarder.execute does not verify req.to equals token before signature check
hypotheses.description: `_verifyNonce` and `_verifySig` are called before the `req.to == _eurfAddress` check. The signature is computed over `req.to`, so a signature for a different `to` will fail the sig check anyway — but the nonce is consumed only after the sig check, so this is not exploitable for replay. However, `verify()` (the view function) performs the same checks but does NOT check `req.to == _eurfAddress`, while `execute()` does. This inconsistency means off-chain callers using `verify()` may accept requests that `execute()` will reject, causing UX/relayer failures.
hypotheses.attackPath: A relayer calls `verify()` off-chain, sees success, submits `execute()`, which reverts on the `req.to` check — wasting gas. Not directly fund-losing but a griefing/DoS vector for relayers.
hypotheses.impact: Relayer gas waste; inconsistent validation between view and state-changing paths.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add the `req.to == _eurfAddress` check to `verify()` as well, or remove it from `execute()` and rely on the signature binding.

hypotheses.title: Forwarder.execute pays gasless basefee after external call enabling reentrancy drain
hypotheses.description: `execute` performs the external call to the token (`req.to.call{...}`) BEFORE calling `_eurf.payGaslessBasefee(req.from, _msgSender())`. The token's `transfer` invokes `_payTxFee` which calls `_update` (state-changing) and can invoke hooks if the token is extended. More importantly, the ordering means the basefee payment is executed after the transfer, so a reentrant call into `execute` (via a malicious `req.to` if `req.to` were attacker-controlled — but here `req.to` is forced to `_eurfAddress`) is limited. However, the token's `transfer` can call back into the forwarder if the recipient is a contract that reenters `execute` with a fresh signature; the nonce for `req.from` was already incremented, so replay is blocked, but the basefee is charged after the transfer, meaning the payer's balance may already be reduced by the transfer, causing `payGaslessBasefee` to revert and the whole tx to revert — or worse, if the token's `_update` triggers a callback, the basefee can be paid twice.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker crafts a signed request where `req.from` is a contract they control. 2) During `transfer`, the recipient contract's fallback reenters `Forwarder.execute` with a different signed request from the same `from` (nonce already consumed, so this fails) — but if the attacker uses a second signer, they can chain. 3) The basefee is paid after the transfer, so the payer's balance check in `payGaslessBasefee` may fail, reverting the entire tx and leaving the token transfer already executed in a prior frame if the token uses a callback.
hypotheses.impact: Inconsistent accounting; potential for basefee to be paid multiple times or for the transfer to succeed while basefee payment reverts, causing DoS or fund loss.
hypotheses.recommendation: Move `_eurf.payGaslessBasefee` before the external call, or use a reentrancy guard and checks-effects-interactions ordering.

hypotheses.title: EURFToken.transferSanity pays tx fee before transfer enabling balance check bypass
hypotheses.description: `transferSanity` calls `_payTxFee(sender, amount)` which performs `_update(from, _feesFaucet, txFees)` BEFORE the actual `super.transfer(recipient, amount)` executes. The balance check in `_payTxFee` is `balanceOf(from) < txFees + txAmount`, which is correct, but the fee is deducted first. If `_feesFaucet` is a contract that reenters `transfer` (e.g., via a callback), the sender's balance is already reduced by the fee, and the reentrant call's balance check uses the reduced balance, potentially allowing a double-fee or a transfer that would otherwise fail. More critically, if `_feesFaucet` is set to a malicious contract, it can reenter `transfer` and drain the sender.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker (as `_feesFaucet`, if they can influence it — but only ADMIN can set it, so this is limited) — however, if `_feesFaucet` is a contract with a fallback that reenters, and the attacker is the recipient, they can trigger reentrancy. 2) The fee is paid first, then the transfer; a reentrant call sees the reduced balance and may pass checks it shouldn't.
hypotheses.impact: Double-charging of fees, incorrect balance accounting, potential drain if `_feesFaucet` is malicious.
hypotheses.recommendation: Perform the transfer first, then the fee, or use a reentrancy guard; ensure `_feesFaucet` cannot reenter.

hypotheses.title: Forwarder.verify is view but nonce check can be bypassed via execute ordering
hypotheses.description: `verify` is a `view` function that checks nonce and signature, but `execute` calls `_verifyNonce` and `_verifySig` then `_updateNonce` before the external call. Since `verify` is view, it cannot be used to consume nonces, but an attacker can call `verify` off-chain to check validity, then front-run the actual `execute` with a higher gas price. The nonce is only incremented in `execute`, so a front-runner can submit the same signed request first, consuming the nonce and causing the victim's `execute` to revert.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker sees a pending `execute` in the mempool. 2) Attacker submits the same `req` with higher gas. 3) Attacker's tx executes first, consuming the nonce and performing the transfer to the attacker's chosen recipient (since `req.to` is fixed to token, but `req.data` encodes recipient). 4) Victim's tx reverts due to nonce mismatch.
hypotheses.impact: Front-running of meta-transactions; the attacker can redirect the transfer if they can alter `req.data` (but signature binds `req.data`, so they cannot). However, they can cause DoS by consuming the nonce.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use a commit-reveal or include a deadline and unique identifier; or accept that front-running is inherent to meta-tx and mitigate with short deadlines.

hypotheses.title: transferSanity double-charges fee check causing revert on exact-balance transfers
hypotheses.description: `transferSanity` calls `_payTxFee(sender, amount)` which requires `balanceOf(from) >= txFees + txAmount`. Then `super.transfer` also transfers `amount`. A user whose balance equals exactly `amount` (no room for fee) will revert even though they intended a fee-inclusive transfer. More importantly, `_payTxFee` is invoked before the actual transfer, so the fee is deducted from the sender's balance and then the full `amount` is transferred — the sender must hold `amount + fee`, not `amount`. This is a liveness issue for users who expect fee-on-transfer semantics.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) User holds exactly `amount` tokens. 2) Calls `transfer(recipient, amount)`. 3) `_payTxFee` reverts with `BalanceTooLow` because `balance < txFees + amount`. 4) Transfer fails; user cannot move their full balance.
hypotheses.impact: Users cannot transfer their entire balance; funds effectively stuck at the margin.
hypotheses.recommendation: Deduct the fee from the transfer amount or document that senders must hold amount+fee.

hypotheses.title: setMasterMinter revokes role from index 0 which may not be the current master
hypotheses.description: `setMasterMinter` reads `getRoleMember(MASTER_MINTER, 0)` to find the former master minter and revokes it. If the role set ever contains more than one member (e.g., via `_grantRole` from a prior admin action or a bug), only index 0 is revoked, leaving stale master minters with full minting power. Conversely, if index 0 is not the intended former master, the wrong account is revoked and the intended one retains MASTER_MINTER, allowing unauthorized minting.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) A stale MASTER_MINTER remains in the role set. 2) `setMasterMinter` revokes only index 0. 3) The stale master can still call `mint` with unlimited allowance, inflating supply.
hypotheses.impact: Unauthorized minting / supply inflation; loss of peg.
hypotheses.recommendation: Iterate and revoke all existing MASTER_MINTER members, or enforce a single-member invariant.

hypotheses.title: safetySwitch can be permanently locked off by controller
hypotheses.description: When `_operating` is true, any CONTROLLER can flip it to false and set `_operatingController` to themselves. To flip back, the caller must be DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE or the stored `_operatingController`. If the controller's key is lost or the controller is removed from CONTROLLER role, only DEFAULT_ADMIN can restore. If DEFAULT_ADMIN is also unavailable, minting and burning are permanently disabled. Additionally, a malicious controller can front-run admin recovery by re-calling `safetySwitch` to reset `_operatingController` to themselves.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Controller calls `safetySwitch()` to set `_operating = false`. 2) Admin attempts to restore; controller front-runs with another `safetySwitch()` (which reverts since already off) — actually the controller cannot re-set while off, but if admin restores, controller can immediately re-disable. 3) Repeated griefing keeps operations off.
hypotheses.impact: Minting/burning permanently disabled; token becomes non-functional for minter operations.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE to restore, or add a timelock on re-disabling.

hypotheses.title: ERC20ControlerMinterUpgradeable.addController/removeController lack access control
hypotheses.description: `addController` and `removeController` call `grantRole`/`revokeRole` without any `onlyRole` modifier. `grantRole` internally checks `_checkRole(getRoleAdmin(role), _msgSender())`, and `CONTROLLER`'s admin is `DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE` (default). So only the admin can actually grant — but the functions are `external` and callable by anyone; the revert happens inside OZ. This is not directly exploitable, but the lack of explicit guard is a footgun. More critically, `setMasterMinter` and `addMinter`/`removeMinter` also lack `onlyRole(MASTER_MINTER)` guards — `addMinter` and `removeMinter` are callable by anyone, and they call `grantRole(MINTER_ROLE, minter)` / `revokeRole`. `MINTER_ROLE`'s admin is `MASTER_MINTER`, so `grantRole` will revert for non-master-minter callers. However, `minterAllowed[minter] = minterAllowedAmount` is set BEFORE the `grantRole` call in `addMinter` — if `grantRole` reverts, the whole tx reverts, so no state change. But `removeMinter` sets `minterAllowed[minter] = 0` before `revokeRole` — same revert behavior. The real issue: `setMasterMinter` has no access control at all and calls `revokeRole(MASTER_MINTER, formerMasterMinter)` and `grantRole(MASTER_MINTER, newMasterMinter)`. `MASTER_MINTER`'s admin is `DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE` (set via `_setRoleAdmin(MINTER_ROLE, MASTER_MINTER)` only sets MINTER_ROLE's admin; MASTER_MINTER's admin remains DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE). So `setMasterMinter` is effectively admin-gated via OZ internals.
hypotheses.attackPath: An untrusted actor calls `addMinter(attacker, type(uint256).max)`. `minterAllowed[attacker]` is set, then `grantRole(MINTER_ROLE, attacker)` reverts because caller lacks MASTER_MINTER. Whole tx reverts. No exploit. Similarly for `removeMinter`. So these are not exploitable.
hypotheses.impact: No direct exploit; the missing modifiers are defense-in-depth issues.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add explicit `onlyRole(MASTER_MINTER)` to `addMinter`, `removeMinter`, `setMasterMinter`, and `onlyRole(DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE)` to `addController`/`removeController`.

hypotheses.title: ERC20MetaTxUpgradeable.transferWithAuthorization uses _update instead of _transfer
hypotheses.description: `transferWithAuthorization` calls `_update(holder, spender, value)` directly, bypassing `_transfer` and any overrides. In `EURFToken`, `transferWithAuthorization` is overridden to call `transferSanity(holder, spender, value)` then `super.transferWithAuthorization(...)`. `transferSanity` calls `_payTxFee` which does `_update(from, _feesFaucet, txFees)` — so fees are paid. But the base `_update` in OZ ERC20 does not check `from` balance beyond the subtraction (which reverts on underflow). The critical issue: `_update` is called with `holder` as `from` and `spender` as `to`, but the signature authorizes `holder` to transfer to `spender`. This is correct semantically. However, `_update` bypasses the `_beforeTokenTransfer`/`_afterTokenTransfer` hooks (in OZ 5.x, `_update` IS the hook). In OZ 5.x, `_transfer` calls `_update`, so this is equivalent. No exploit here.
hypotheses.attackPath: N/A — `_update` is the correct internal function in OZ 5.x.
hypotheses.impact: None.
hypotheses.recommendation: None needed; verify OZ version compatibility.

hypotheses.title: EURFToken.payGaslessBasefee trusts msg.sender not _msgSender
hypotheses.description: `payGaslessBasefee` checks `isTrustedForwarder(msg.sender)` — using raw `msg.sender`, not `_msgSender()`. The Forwarder calls `_eurf.payGaslessBasefee(req.from, _msgSender())` directly (not via meta-tx), so `msg.sender` is the Forwarder contract. This works only if the Forwarder is set as the trusted forwarder. But `_msgSender()` in the token would interpret calldata suffix if `msg.sender` is the trusted forwarder — here `msg.sender` IS the forwarder, so `_msgSender()` would read the last 20 bytes of calldata, which is `paymaster` (the second arg). This is not used. The check `isTrustedForwarder(msg.sender)` is correct for this direct call pattern. However, if the token is called via meta-tx (forwarder → token), `msg.sender` is the forwarder and the check passes. No exploit.
hypotheses.attackPath: N/A.
hypotheses.impact: None.
hypotheses.recommendation: None.

hypotheses.title: EURFToken.initialize does not call __ERC20ControlerMinter_init or __ERC20Admin_init
hypotheses.description: `EURFToken.initialize()` calls `__ERC20_init_unchained`, `__ERC20MetaTx_init_unchained`, `__ERC20Admin_init_unchained`, and `__ERC20ControlerMinter_init_unchained` — but NOT the full `__ERC20ControlerMinter_init` or `__ERC20Admin_init`. The unchained versions are called directly. `__ERC20ControlerMinter_init_unchained` sets `_setRoleAdmin(MINTER_ROLE, MASTER_MINTER)` and `_grantRole(MASTER_MINTER, address(0))`. `__ERC20Admin_init_unchained` grants `ADMIN` to `address(0)`. These are called, so roles are set. However, `__ERC20MetaTx_init_unchained` sets `_PERMIT_TYPEHASH` and `_TWA_TYPEHASH` — called. `__EIP712_init("EURF", "1")` is called. The issue: `__ERC20_init_unchained("EURF", "EURF")` is called, but `__ERC20_init` (which calls `__ERC20_init_unchained`) is not — this is fine since unchained is called directly. The real problem: `__Pausable_init()` is called, `__AccessControlEnumerable_init()` is called, `__UUPSUpgradeable_init()` is called. All good. But `__ERC20ControlerMinter_init` (the full one) is NOT called — only unchained. The full one calls `__ERC20_init` and `__AccessControlEnumerable_init` again, which would revert if called twice. So calling unchained directly is correct. No exploit.
hypotheses.attackPath: N/A.
hypotheses.impact: None.
hypotheses.recommendation: None.

hypotheses.title: forceTransfer bypasses fee accounting, enabling fee-free transfers by admin
hypotheses.description: `forceTransfer` calls `adminSanity` and `_update` directly, bypassing `_payTxFee`. While admin is trusted, the function is exposed and any compromised or malicious admin key can move tokens without fees, and more importantly the fee accounting (`FeesPaid` events, faucet balance) is inconsistent with normal transfers. This creates an economic asymmetry where admin-controlled transfers avoid the protocol's fee mechanism entirely.
hypotheses.attackPath: Not exploitable by untrusted actor directly; requires admin role. Excluded per rules unless admin is considered untrusted — not applicable.
hypotheses.impact: Fee evasion by privileged role; inconsistent accounting.
hypotheses.recommendation: Apply `_payTxFee` in `forceTransfer` or document the exemption explicitly.

hypotheses.title: setMasterMinter grants unlimited allowance without resetting previous minter allowance
hypotheses.description: `setMasterMinter` revokes `MASTER_MINTER` from the former holder and grants it to the new one, but does not reset `minterAllowed` for the former master minter. Since `mint` checks `hasRole(MASTER_MINTER)` first and skips the allowance check for master minters, the former master minter loses minting rights — but if they also hold `MINTER_ROLE`, their stale `minterAllowed` remains. More critically, the new master minter gets unlimited minting without any allowance tracking, and the old master minter's `minterAllowed` mapping is never zeroed, leaving stale state.
hypotheses.attackPath: Not directly exploitable by untrusted actor; requires admin. Excluded.
hypotheses.impact: Stale allowance state; potential confusion in accounting.
hypotheses.recommendation: Zero out `minterAllowed[formerMasterMinter]` when revoking.
